families.name: Physical cores
families.description: A seed, an inner part, or a starting region.

families.name: What a map collapses
families.description: Inputs sent to zero, or inputs a map identifies.

families.name: Weights & influences
families.description: A function or neighborhood that describes an operation.

families.name: Inner products & similarity
families.description: Pairwise functions with additional mathematical structure.

families.name: Distinguished subsets
families.description: A region or subset picked out by a defining property.

families.name: Executable computations
families.description: A routine that performs a computational operation.

families.name: Core engines
families.description: The central machinery of a software system.

families.name: Reduced problems
families.description: A smaller instance with a formal preservation guarantee.

families.name: Spacecraft data
families.description: A SPICE file containing mission geometry or supporting data.

entries.name: Grain kernel
entries.short: The grain itself, including its seed tissues.
entries.body: In cereals, a kernel is a grain: botanically a caryopsis, a fruit whose wall is closely joined to the seed coat. A corn kernel contains protective outer tissues, endosperm and an embryo (germ).
entries.example: A maize kernel contains a developing plant and stored food. Milling separates useful fractions such as germ, starch and fiber.
entries.note: A corn kernel is not just the germ. Likewise, an acorn is a whole nut; its inner seed can be called its kernel.

entries.name: Nut kernel
entries.short: The seed or edible inner part inside a shell.
entries.body: In nut processing, kernel names the inner seed material recovered when the shell is removed. Everyday culinary categories need not match botanical categories.
entries.example: Crack a walnut: the lobed seed inside is the walnut kernel. Kernel color, shriveling and recovery yield are quality measurements.
entries.note: An almond is botanically the seed of a drupe; the culinary label nut does not change what processors mean by kernel.

entries.name: Atomic kernel
entries.short: An atom's inner core, excluding its outer electrons.
entries.body: Lewis's 1916 account distinguishes an inner kernel from an outer electron shell. In this terminology, the kernel comprises the nucleus and inner electrons; valence electrons lie outside it.
entries.example: For carbon in a simple shell picture, the nucleus and two inner electrons form a core with net charge +4; four valence electrons sit outside.
entries.note: This is historical chemical language. Kernel is not the usual modern name for an atomic nucleus, and Lewis's original atom model is not modern quantum mechanics.

entries.name: Flame / ignition kernel
entries.short: A small ignition region that may grow into a flame.
entries.body: A localized heated or reacting region initiates combustion. A successful ignition kernel develops into a self-sustaining flame; a weak one can be extinguished by heat loss or stretching.
entries.example: A spark in an engine creates a small hot region. Whether that region survives and grows helps determine whether ignition succeeds.
entries.note: Here kernel is a physical region, not a numerical filter used to simulate combustion.

entries.name: Nuclear fuel kernel
entries.short: The fuel-bearing core of a coated particle.
entries.body: A TRISO particle encloses a small fuel kernel, commonly uranium dioxide or uranium oxycarbide, within protective carbon and silicon-carbide layers.
entries.example: In a coated fuel particle, fission occurs in the fuel-bearing core; the surrounding layers retain fission products and protect the core.
entries.note: This is a material component. A radiation point kernel is instead a mathematical response function.

entries.name: Linear-algebra kernel
entries.short: Every vector a linear map sends to zero.
entries.body: The kernel, or nullspace, of a linear map A is the subspace of inputs x satisfying Ax = 0. It records directions that the map loses.
entries.example: For A = [1  2], every vector t(−2, 1) maps to zero. The kernel is a line, not the zero vector alone.
entries.note: A matrix used as an image filter is also called a kernel, but its nullspace is a different object.

entries.name: Group-homomorphism kernel
entries.short: Group elements sent to the identity.
entries.body: For a group homomorphism φ, the kernel is the preimage of the target group's identity. It is a normal subgroup; quotienting by it removes exactly the distinctions that φ loses.
entries.example: Reduction modulo 3 maps the additive group of integers to ℤ/3ℤ. Its kernel is 3ℤ.
entries.note: Zero is the identity for additive groups. For multiplicative groups, use the identity 1 instead.

entries.name: Ring-homomorphism kernel
entries.short: Ring elements sent to zero; an ideal.
entries.body: The zero fiber of a ring homomorphism is an ideal. In algebraic geometry, such kernels can encode equations imposed by a map of coordinate rings.
entries.example: Evaluation at 2 sends a polynomial p(x) to p(2). Over ℝ[x], its kernel is the ideal generated by x−2.
entries.note: In the category of unital rings, the zero map is generally not a unital morphism. The ideal kernel and the categorical zero-map construction need care.

entries.name: Module / Lie-algebra kernel
entries.short: A submodule or ideal consisting of zero-mapped elements.
entries.body: A module homomorphism's zero fiber is a submodule. A Lie-algebra homomorphism's zero fiber is a Lie ideal. These are algebraic versions of the same map-to-zero idea.
entries.example: The homomorphism ℤ → ℤ/4ℤ has kernel 4ℤ, viewed as a ℤ-submodule of ℤ.
entries.note: Different ambient algebraic structures impose different closure properties on the kernel.

entries.name: Differential-operator kernel
entries.short: Functions annihilated by an operator.
entries.body: The nullspace idea also applies to spaces of functions. The kernel of a differential operator consists of solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, in a specified function space and with any imposed boundary conditions.
entries.example: On an interval, the kernel of d/dx consists of constant functions. The kernel of the Laplacian consists of harmonic functions.
entries.note: A Green kernel represents a solution operator; it is not the nullspace of the differential operator. Domains and boundary conditions matter.

entries.name: Congruence / function kernel
entries.short: Pairs of inputs that have the same output.
entries.body: Another convention calls the equivalence relation f(x)=f(y) the kernel of f. For a homomorphism of universal algebras, this relation is compatible with the algebra's operations: a congruence.
entries.example: For f(n)=n mod 3, the relation groups integers into three equivalence classes. It contains every pair differing by a multiple of 3.
entries.note: This kernel is a set of pairs, not just the zero equivalence class 3ℤ.

entries.name: Categorical kernel
entries.short: A universal arrow on which a morphism becomes zero.
entries.body: In a category with zero morphisms, a kernel of f:A→B is an arrow k:K→A that equalizes f and the zero arrow, with the corresponding universal property.
entries.example: For vector spaces, K is the usual nullspace and k includes it into A. Every map g with fg=0 factors uniquely through k.
entries.note: The categorical kernel includes a morphism and a universal property. Not every category has zero arrows or kernels.

entries.name: Kernel pair
entries.short: The pullback that records inputs identified by a map.
entries.body: Where the relevant pullback exists, the kernel pair of f:A→B is A×ᵦA with its two projections to A. In sets it consists of pairs with equal f-images.
entries.example: The kernel pair of reduction modulo 3 records two integers whenever their residues agree.
entries.note: A kernel pair need not require a zero object. It generalizes the relation kernel, rather than the zero fiber alone.

entries.name: Isogeny kernel
entries.short: Points mapped to the identity of another elliptic curve.
entries.body: An isogeny is a suitable group-preserving algebraic map between elliptic curves. Its point kernel over an algebraic closure is finite. For separable isogenies, the finite subgroup determines the quotient isogeny up to isomorphism.
entries.example: Over characteristic zero, the doubling map [2] has the identity and three nonzero 2-torsion points in its kernel.
entries.note: In positive characteristic, inseparability makes the distinction between geometric points and the kernel group scheme important.

entries.name: Parity-check kernel
entries.short: The nullspace describing all valid codewords.
entries.body: A linear code can be specified as the vectors annihilated by a parity-check matrix H over a finite field.
entries.example: Over 𝔽₂, H=[1 1 1] defines {000, 011, 101, 110}: exactly the binary triples with even parity.
entries.note: Arithmetic is in the stated finite field, not ordinary real arithmetic. This is a use of the linear-algebra kernel.

entries.name: Integral-operator kernel
entries.short: The two-variable function specifying an integral operator.
entries.body: A function K(x,y) describes how an input value at y contributes to an output at x. The operator integrates those contributions. More generally, a Schwartz kernel can be a distribution rather than an ordinary function.
entries.example: For K(x,y)=xy on [0,1] and f(y)=y, the output is x∫₀¹y²dy=x/3.
entries.note: The function K and the nullspace ker(T) are both called kernels, even in the same discussion.

entries.name: Convolution kernel
entries.short: A translated weighting function.
entries.body: Convolution is the translation-invariant case of an integral operator: K(x,y)=k(x−y). A single function k describes how the signal is mixed at every location.
entries.example: A normalized box kernel averages nearby values. An impulse convolved with k reproduces k.
entries.note: Mathematical convolution reverses one operand relative to cross-correlation. Symmetric kernels hide this difference.

entries.name: Discrete image / signal kernel
entries.short: A small array of filter coefficients.
entries.body: A finite collection of weights samples the neighborhood around each output location. Blur, sharpening, derivatives and edge detection use different weight patterns.
entries.example: The centered filter [¼, ½, ¼] changes a neighborhood [2, 8, 2] into the weighted value 5.
entries.note: Padding, origin, stride and whether the array is flipped affect the result. A filter need not be positive or normalized.

entries.name: CNN kernel / learned filter
entries.short: A learned tensor of local filter weights.
entries.body: A convolution layer learns weights shared across spatial positions. With multiple channels, each output filter combines neighborhoods from the relevant input channels.
entries.example: An ordinary Conv2d with 3 input channels, 8 output channels and 3×3 filters has weights shaped 8×3×3×3: 216 numbers, plus optional biases.
entries.note: PyTorch Conv2d implements cross-correlation. These weight tensors are distinct from the executable CPU or GPU kernels that apply them.

entries.name: Morphological kernel
entries.short: A neighborhood shape, also called a structuring element.
entries.body: In morphology APIs, kernel often means a mask selecting the neighborhood for erosion, dilation, opening or closing. These operations need not be weighted sums.
entries.example: For binary dilation, a cross-shaped neighborhood expands a set in its four cardinal directions.
entries.note: A morphological kernel usually describes a shape or footprint. It is not generally a linear convolution filter.

entries.name: Transform kernel
entries.short: The function against which a transform integrates.
entries.body: Integral transforms change a function's representation by integrating it against a prescribed function of the input and output coordinates.
entries.example: The Fourier kernel is e⁻²πⁱˣξ in this convention; the one-sided Laplace kernel is e⁻ˢᵗ on t≥0.
entries.note: A transform kernel may oscillate, be complex-valued, and have no probability or similarity interpretation. Fourier normalization conventions vary.

entries.name: Green kernel / Green's function
entries.short: The response to a point source, with boundary conditions.
entries.body: A Green kernel represents an inverse or solution operator for a differential equation. Integrating the point-source responses builds the response to a distributed source.
entries.example: For −u″=f on (0,1) with u(0)=u(1)=0, G(x,y)=min(x,y)−xy; then u(x)=∫₀¹G(x,y)f(y)dy.
entries.note: The operator, domain and boundary conditions are part of the definition. A Green kernel and an operator's nullspace are different.

entries.name: Heat / diffusion kernel
entries.short: How a point concentration spreads over time.
entries.body: For heat diffusion in ℝᵈ, the fundamental solution is a normalized Gaussian whose width grows with time. Convolving it with initial data solves the homogeneous heat equation.
entries.example: In one dimension, the distribution represented by Hₜ has variance 2Dt. More elapsed time produces a wider, lower peak.
entries.note: A heat kernel is a convolution kernel and, in suitable settings, a transition density. On a general manifold it is not a simple Gaussian of coordinate distance.

entries.name: Poisson kernel
entries.short: Weights that extend boundary values harmonically.
entries.body: A Poisson kernel solves a harmonic boundary-value problem by weighting boundary data. Its form depends on the domain.
entries.example: In the unit disk, integrate Pᵣ against boundary values using dθ/(2π). At r=0, every boundary angle has equal weight.
entries.note: This Poisson kernel is unrelated to Poisson-distributed counts except through broader probabilistic connections.

entries.name: Dirichlet kernel
entries.short: The convolution kernel for a Fourier partial sum.
entries.body: Adding the frequency modes from −N through N produces a kernel that reconstructs the Nth Fourier partial sum.
entries.example: D₁(θ)=1+2cosθ. Its oscillating lobes help explain why partial sums can overshoot near jumps.
entries.note: It is not everywhere positive and is not a probability density. Its name does not make it the general kernel for a Dirichlet boundary problem.

entries.name: Fejér kernel
entries.short: The nonnegative kernel for averaged Fourier sums.
entries.body: Averaging the first N+1 Dirichlet kernels gives a nonnegative approximation kernel with good convergence properties for continuous periodic functions.
entries.example: For N=1, F₁(θ)=1+cosθ. Its integral with normalized circle measure is 1.
entries.note: Cesàro averaging changes the kernel, rather than simply adding more Fourier modes.

entries.name: Mollifier / approximate-identity kernel
entries.short: A scaled kernel that smooths while approaching the identity.
entries.body: A standard mollifier is a smooth, nonnegative, unit-integral bump. Shrinking its scale gives a family whose convolution approximates the original function. Approximate identities form a broader class.
entries.example: Convolving a step with a small smooth bump replaces the jump with a narrow smooth transition.
entries.note: Not every smoothing filter is an approximate identity, and not every approximate identity is a compactly supported smooth mollifier.

entries.name: Singular / Calderón–Zygmund kernel
entries.short: An operator kernel singular along the diagonal.
entries.body: Singular integral kernels can blow up as x approaches y. Cancellation, principal values and suitable boundedness and regularity conditions make the corresponding operators meaningful.
entries.example: The Hilbert-transform kernel is the one-dimensional prototype. Riesz transforms provide higher-dimensional examples.
entries.note: An arbitrary divergent integral is not automatically a valid singular integral operator.

entries.name: Hilbert-transform kernel
entries.short: A principal-value 1/x kernel.
entries.body: The Hilbert transform uses an odd singular kernel to construct a quadrature counterpart of a real signal. Its convolution is interpreted in the principal-value sense.
entries.example: In a standard convention, H(cosωx)=sinωx for ω>0. This is useful in analytic-signal representations.
entries.note: Normalization and sign conventions vary. This is not the reproducing kernel of an arbitrary Hilbert space.

entries.name: Cauchy kernel
entries.short: The reciprocal kernel in Cauchy's integral formula.
entries.body: Cauchy's formula recovers a holomorphic function from its values on a surrounding contour by integrating against a reciprocal factor.
entries.example: For f(ζ)=ζ² on a contour surrounding z, the integral returns z².
entries.note: The contour orientation and the location of z matter. A Cauchy kernel is not the same object as a Cauchy probability density.

entries.name: Density-estimation kernel
entries.short: A normalized bump placed at each observation.
entries.body: Kernel density estimation adds rescaled copies of a kernel around observed samples to estimate a density. Bandwidth sets the smoothing scale.
entries.example: Place one Gaussian bump at each sample, then average the bumps. Smaller h reveals more detail and more sample noise.
entries.note: A classical density kernel integrates to 1. It need not be a positive-semidefinite similarity kernel; higher-order estimation kernels can even have negative parts.

entries.name: Kernel-regression weights
entries.short: Weights for fitting or averaging nearby observations.
entries.body: In Nadaraya–Watson regression, a kernel assigns locality weights and their normalized sum gives a predicted mean. Local polynomial regression uses related weights in a local fit.
entries.example: If two response values 10 and 20 receive weights 3 and 1, the local constant prediction is 12.5.
entries.note: This local smoother differs from kernel ridge regression in an RKHS, although both may use Gaussian functions.

entries.name: Interpolation / reconstruction kernel
entries.short: A function used to reconstruct values between samples.
entries.body: A reconstruction kernel builds a continuous approximation from discrete samples. The kernel shape controls sharpness, smoothness and ringing.
entries.example: A triangular kernel gives linear interpolation in one dimension. Ideal bandlimited reconstruction uses sinc(x)=sin(πx)/(πx).
entries.note: Exact sinc reconstruction requires the sampling theorem's assumptions. Bicubic and Lanczos filters are practical alternatives with different tradeoffs.

entries.name: Measure / probability kernel
entries.short: A measurable assignment of a measure to each input.
entries.body: A measure kernel assigns a measure K(x,·) to every x, measurably in x. A probability kernel assigns probability measures. Densities are optional, not part of the general definition.
entries.example: K(x,B)=δₓ(B) describes deterministic copying of x: all probability is concentrated at x.
entries.note: K(x,B) takes a measurable set as its second argument. A density k(x,y), when one exists, is a representation of this kernel.

entries.name: Markov transition kernel
entries.short: The distribution of the next state, given the current state.
entries.body: A transition kernel specifies a Markov step. On a finite state space, it is a nonnegative row-stochastic matrix; on general spaces it is a probability kernel.
entries.example: For P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], state 0 transitions to state 1 with probability 0.2. Every row sums to 1.
entries.note: A Markov kernel need not be symmetric or positive semidefinite. An SVM kernel has different requirements.

entries.name: Density / likelihood kernel
entries.short: A density or likelihood with irrelevant constants removed.
entries.body: In statistical calculations, kernel can mean the part of a density or likelihood left after factors constant in the variable of interest are dropped.
entries.example: For a normal density with fixed variance, viewed as a function of μ, exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)) is its likelihood kernel.
entries.note: Constant means constant in the variable being studied. If σ is unknown, the 1/σ factor cannot be discarded.

entries.name: Stein kernel: integration by parts
entries.short: A function or matrix realizing a Stein identity.
entries.body: For a one-dimensional variable X with mean μ, a Stein kernel τ satisfies an integration-by-parts identity for suitable test functions.
entries.example: For X∼N(μ,σ²), the constant τ(x)=σ² is a Stein kernel. For a uniform variable on [−1,1], τ(x)=(1−x²)/2.
entries.note: This τ is a function of one input. The pairwise Stein kernel used in a kernel Stein discrepancy is another construction.

entries.name: Volterra-series kernel
entries.short: A higher-order impulse-response function.
entries.body: A Volterra expansion expresses a nonlinear system through kernels of one, two or more time lags, multiplying corresponding input values before integration.
entries.example: A quadratic response requires a two-lag kernel h₂, whereas an LTI system uses a one-lag impulse response h₁.
entries.note: Volterra can also describe a linear integral operator with a variable integration limit. That usage is an integral-kernel subtype.

entries.name: Memory / friction kernel
entries.short: Weights on the system's past behavior.
entries.body: A memory kernel specifies how past states or velocities influence present evolution. Generalized Langevin equations use such kernels to describe non-instantaneous friction.
entries.example: With Γ(t)=γe⁻ᵗ/τ, recent velocities receive greater weight than distant ones.
entries.note: This is a temporal response function, not a block of computer memory or a GPU routine.

entries.name: Dispersal kernel
entries.short: A distribution of dispersal displacement or distance.
entries.body: A dispersal kernel describes where seeds, spores or organisms arrive relative to their source. Its tails strongly affect long-range spread.
entries.example: A narrow Gaussian models mostly local movement; a heavy-tailed distribution allows more rare long-distance arrivals.
entries.note: A distance density and a density per unit area differ by a radial Jacobian. Always check the units and normalization.

entries.name: Collision / coagulation kernel
entries.short: A rate describing pair interactions.
entries.body: A coagulation kernel K(a,b) gives the rate at which particles of sizes a and b merge in a population-balance model. Collision kernels in kinetic equations likewise encode interaction rates.
entries.example: The constant coagulation kernel assigns the same size-independent rate to every pair; additive and multiplicative kernels weight sizes differently.
entries.note: Nonnegative interaction rates do not imply a positive-semidefinite ML kernel. Physical units are rate units, not similarity units.

entries.name: Sensitivity / Fréchet kernel
entries.short: How a model perturbation changes an observation.
entries.body: Linearizing a forward model produces a sensitivity kernel: a spatial weighting of parameter perturbations that predicts a small data change.
entries.example: A seismic travel-time kernel indicates which regions of Earth's structure influence a measurement. Finite-frequency sensitivity can occupy a volume rather than a single ray.
entries.note: It represents a derivative of the forward model, not necessarily the resolution of a retrieved model.

entries.name: Averaging / resolution kernel
entries.short: How the true state appears in a retrieved state.
entries.body: An averaging kernel differentiates the retrieval with respect to the true state. It describes sensitivity and smoothing in a recovered atmospheric profile or other inverse solution.
entries.example: A retrieved value at one altitude may average the true state over nearby altitudes. An ideal noiseless, fully resolved retrieval has A=I.
entries.note: Averaging kernels need not be simple positive averages. They differ from the forward measurement's sensitivity kernel.

entries.name: Radiation point kernel
entries.short: The detector response to a point radiation source.
entries.body: Point-kernel methods integrate point-source responses over a distributed radiation source. A basic uncollided photon-flux term combines geometric spreading and attenuation; buildup models can approximate scattered contributions.
entries.example: In a homogeneous absorber, the uncollided response falls with inverse-square distance and exponential attenuation.
entries.note: Real shielding calculations require energy, material, geometry and scattering considerations. This formula is an illustrative idealization, not a shield-design prescription.

entries.name: Exchange–correlation kernel
entries.short: A functional derivative of a potential with respect to density.
entries.body: The exchange–correlation response kernel relates a small electron-density change to a change in the exchange–correlation potential.
entries.example: An adiabatic local approximation yields a response local in time and space, represented using delta factors and a density-dependent derivative.
entries.note: This is a response function in density-functional theory, not the core electrons of the historical atomic kernel.

entries.name: Bethe–Salpeter interaction kernel
entries.short: The interaction part of a two-particle integral equation.
entries.body: The Bethe–Salpeter framework uses an interaction kernel to couple two-particle amplitudes. Approximations to it determine which interaction contributions the model includes.
entries.example: A ladder approximation retains repeated exchanges built from an elementary exchange kernel.
entries.note: This is a schematic operator equation; propagator factors, indices and integration conventions vary by formulation.

entries.name: Kernel polynomial method
entries.short: A damping kernel for truncated polynomial expansions.
entries.body: Kernel polynomial methods damp coefficients of truncated Chebyshev expansions to reduce oscillations and obtain useful spectral approximations.
entries.example: Jackson damping suppresses ringing in approximate densities of states. Dirichlet and Lorentz kernels give other damping choices.
entries.note: The displayed series omits application-specific prefactors and normalization. The kernel concerns the expansion, not GPU execution.

entries.name: SPH smoothing kernel
entries.short: A spatial weighting function for particle-based fields.
entries.body: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics approximates continuum fields through a smoothing kernel and particle sums. Smoothing length and kernel shape determine which neighbors contribute and how strongly.
entries.example: A compactly supported spline kernel lets a particle gather information from a finite neighborhood rather than from the entire simulation.
entries.note: The smoothing kernel is a mathematical function. A GPU kernel can execute the particle sum; these are different layers.

entries.name: Generating-function kernel
entries.short: The coefficient canceled in the kernel method.
entries.body: In functional equations for generating functions, a kernel is a coefficient multiplying the unknown function. The kernel method selects a suitable root that cancels this coefficient and exposes a relation among remaining terms.
entries.example: For a walk step polynomial P(u)=u+u⁻¹, a common kernel is 1−zP(u). One chooses a formal root with the required behavior near z=0.
entries.note: A root cannot be chosen arbitrarily: formal-series and analyticity conditions matter. This kernel method is not machine-learning kernel fitting.

entries.name: Positive-semidefinite kernel
entries.short: A pairwise function whose Gram matrices are PSD.
entries.body: For a real symmetric kernel k, every finite Gram matrix must be positive semidefinite. This makes k representable as an inner product in a feature space.
entries.example: The ordinary dot product is a kernel: k(x,y)=xᵀy. More elaborate kernels let algorithms use implicit feature spaces.
entries.note: A plausible similarity score is not automatically a valid PSD kernel. Literature often says positive definite while allowing semidefinite Gram matrices.

entries.name: Reproducing kernel
entries.short: A pairwise function that reproduces evaluation.
entries.body: In a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, evaluation is an inner product with a distinguished kernel section. Every positive-semidefinite kernel determines an associated RKHS.
entries.example: If k(x,y)=xy on ℝ, the associated functions have the form f(x)=ax; pairing with k(x,·) recovers ax.
entries.note: Not every Hilbert space of functions is an RKHS: point evaluation must be a bounded functional.

entries.name: Covariance kernel
entries.short: The covariance between indexed random variables.
entries.body: A covariance kernel expresses how fluctuations at two inputs co-vary. For a Gaussian process, a mean function and a valid covariance kernel specify all finite-dimensional distributions.
entries.example: A long length scale in an RBF covariance makes nearby observations strongly correlated; a shorter scale allows faster variation.
entries.note: A covariance may be negative at some pairs while its Gram matrices remain PSD. Positive entrywise values and positive semidefiniteness are different properties.

entries.name: Gaussian / RBF similarity kernel
entries.short: Exponentially decreasing similarity in squared distance.
entries.body: The Gaussian radial-basis-function kernel compares points using their squared Euclidean distance and a scale parameter. It is a standard PSD kernel.
entries.example: At distance ℓ, similarity is e⁻¹/²≈0.607. At zero distance it is 1.
entries.note: The same Gaussian shape appears in heat flow, KDE and image blur. Their arguments, units and normalization differ.

entries.name: Named similarity-kernel families
entries.short: Different constructions inside the PSD family.
entries.body: Linear, polynomial, Laplacian, Matérn, rational-quadratic and periodic kernels encode different notions of features, smoothness or repetition.
entries.example: For γ=1, c=0 and d=2, the polynomial kernel equals the dot product of quadratic feature vectors.
entries.note: Parameters and domains matter. The sigmoid formula tanh(γxᵀy+c), although offered by software APIs, is not PSD for arbitrary parameters.

entries.name: Graph kernel: machine learning
entries.short: A similarity kernel between whole graphs.
entries.body: Graph kernels use features such as walks, subgraphs or neighborhood patterns to compare graph-structured inputs within kernel methods.
entries.example: A simple kernel compares vectors counting vertex labels. Richer kernels compare shared walks or Weisfeiler–Lehman patterns.
entries.note: A graph-theory kernel is a selected vertex set in a single digraph; a graph ML kernel compares two graph objects.

entries.name: String / sequence kernel
entries.short: An inner-product comparison of sequence features.
entries.body: String kernels compare sequences through features such as counts of substrings or subsequences, often without explicitly constructing the full feature vectors.
entries.example: For length-2 substring counts, AABA has AA, AB and BA once each. Comparing these counts gives a simple spectrum kernel.
entries.note: This is a similarity function for sequences, not a text-processing routine or language runtime.

entries.name: Fisher kernel
entries.short: Similarity between model-score vectors.
entries.body: A generative model provides score features: gradients of log likelihood with respect to its parameters. The Fisher kernel compares those features using an information-based metric.
entries.example: Two observations are similar when they suggest similar parameter changes in the chosen generative model.
entries.note: The model and parameterization are part of the construction; an inverse or suitable generalized inverse requires care.

entries.name: Neural tangent kernel
entries.short: Inner products of parameter gradients.
entries.body: For a scalar network output, the NTK compares gradients of the output with respect to model parameters. It describes local function changes during training.
entries.example: For fθ(x)=θx, the NTK is xy. For a finite nonlinear network, it generally changes as θ changes.
entries.note: The limiting constant-kernel training description requires specific infinite-width assumptions. An arbitrary finite network is not automatically in that regime.

entries.name: Neural-network GP kernel
entries.short: Output covariance from a random network.
entries.body: Randomly initialized networks can induce covariance kernels. Under suitable infinite-width conditions, their outputs converge to a Gaussian process with a network-dependent kernel.
entries.example: For fθ(x)=θx with θ∼N(0,1), the induced covariance is xy.
entries.note: The NNGP kernel uses random outputs; the NTK uses parameter gradients. Their roles and formulas differ.

entries.name: Kernel mean / distribution embedding
entries.short: Represent a distribution by an average kernel section.
entries.body: A kernel mean embedding averages feature representations under a distribution. Distances between such embeddings produce the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).
entries.example: With a linear kernel, the embedding captures the ordinary mean. A characteristic kernel can distinguish all probability distributions in an appropriate class.
entries.note: Kernel here is still the underlying pairwise PSD function; the mean embedding is a derived object. Moment and measurability assumptions apply.

entries.name: Stein kernel: pairwise discrepancy
entries.short: An RKHS kernel transformed by Stein operators.
entries.body: Applying a distribution's Stein operator to both arguments of a base kernel produces a pairwise kernel used to assess sample fit, often without a density's normalizing constant.
entries.example: A kernel Stein discrepancy combines density scores and derivatives of an RBF kernel to compare a sample with a model.
entries.note: This pairwise function is distinct from the one-input integration-by-parts Stein kernel τ(x). Boundary and regularity conditions matter.

entries.name: Quantum feature kernel
entries.short: Similarity defined by encoded quantum states.
entries.body: A quantum feature map encodes an input into a state. A common kernel is the squared overlap of two encoded states, also interpretable as an inner product of density operators.
entries.example: Identical pure states give similarity 1; orthogonal states give 0.
entries.note: This is a kernel method implemented or estimated with quantum circuits. A useful quantum advantage does not follow merely from the definition.

entries.name: Bergman kernel
entries.short: The reproducing kernel for square-integrable holomorphic functions.
entries.body: The Bergman kernel reproduces holomorphic functions in an L² space on a complex domain and represents the Bergman projection.
entries.example: On the unit disk with ordinary area measure, integrating B(z,w)f(w) over the disk recovers f(z) for suitable holomorphic f.
entries.note: The domain and measure normalization determine the formula. It is both an integral kernel and a reproducing kernel.

entries.name: Szegő kernel
entries.short: A reproducing kernel for a Hardy-space setting.
entries.body: The Szegő kernel reproduces functions in a Hardy space, using boundary rather than area-based data in the standard disk setting.
entries.example: With normalized boundary measure dθ/(2π), the disk Hardy-space kernel is 1/(1−z w̄).
entries.note: Normalization varies. The Szegő and Bergman kernels reproduce different function spaces; they are not interchangeable.

entries.name: Determinantal / correlation kernel
entries.short: A kernel whose determinants encode joint point correlations.
entries.body: Determinantal point processes express their correlation functions as determinants of matrices built from a kernel. Famous scaling limits include the sine, Airy and Bessel kernels.
entries.example: The sine kernel is sin(π(x−y))/(π(x−y)), with diagonal value 1, in a common bulk-scaling convention.
entries.note: Not every PSD kernel defines a valid determinantal process. Operator constraints and the reference measure also matter.

entries.name: Attention kernel / feature map
entries.short: A pairwise weighting expressed using kernel features.
entries.body: Kernel formulations of attention express pairwise weights through feature maps. Associativity can then rearrange some attention computations to avoid explicitly forming every pairwise weight.
entries.example: A nonnegative feature map can give usable attention weights, followed by row normalization and a weighted sum of value vectors.
entries.note: Distinct query/key projections and row normalization generally do not produce a symmetric PSD token matrix. Not every attention score is a Mercer kernel.

entries.name: Digraph kernel
entries.short: An independent, absorbing set of vertices.
entries.body: A digraph kernel is a vertex set with no arcs between its members, such that every vertex outside it has an outgoing arc to a member.
entries.tex: \forall v\notin K\;\exists k\in K:\ v\to k
entries.example: For the chain a→b→c, {a,c} is a kernel: it is independent, and b points to c. A directed 3-cycle has no kernel.
entries.note: Absorption uses outgoing arcs in this convention. A maximal independent set alone is insufficient in a directed graph.

entries.name: Visibility kernel
entries.short: All points that can see the entire shape.
entries.body: The kernel of a polygon or suitable polyhedron consists of points from which every point of the shape is visible along a segment staying inside it.
entries.example: A convex polygon's kernel is the whole polygon. For a simple star-shaped polygon, intersect the interior half-planes of its edges.
entries.note: The kernel can be empty. A CGAL geometry kernel is software machinery, not this visible region.

entries.name: Viability kernel
entries.short: Initial states from which some safe evolution exists.
entries.body: Within a constraint set, the viability kernel contains states for which at least one admissible evolution stays in the set for the specified horizon, often forever.
entries.example: For a vehicle near a wall, safety depends on position and velocity: some positions are already unrecoverable if the vehicle is moving too quickly.
entries.note: This is an existence guarantee under a model and control constraints. It does not mean every possible control is safe.

entries.name: Discriminating / robust safety kernel
entries.short: States from which safety can be maintained against disturbances.
entries.body: A discriminating kernel strengthens viability by introducing a disturbance or opponent. Safety must be preserved using an appropriate control strategy under the stated information pattern.
entries.example: A robot's safe region shrinks when the model must tolerate an adversarial wind rather than one favorable wind trajectory.
entries.note: Quantifier order, when disturbances are observed, and strategy definitions are essential. Robust-control terminology varies across formulations.

entries.name: Perfect kernel
entries.short: The perfect part left after removing isolated points.
entries.body: Cantor–Bendixson analysis repeatedly removes isolated points, possibly through transfinite stages. In a Polish-space setting, the remaining perfect part is called the perfect kernel.
entries.tex: X=P\sqcup C,\quad P\text{ perfect},\ C\text{ countable}
entries.example: For the Cantor set together with one isolated point outside it, the perfect kernel is the Cantor set.
entries.note: Perfect means closed with no isolated points. Removing isolated points only once need not reach the perfect kernel.

entries.name: Topological set kernel
entries.short: The intersection of all open supersets of a set.
entries.body: Some topology literature calls the saturation of A its kernel: the points that cannot be excluded by any open set containing A.
entries.example: In the Sierpiński space with open sets ∅, {1}, {0,1}, the kernel of {0} is {0,1}.
entries.note: This construction can enlarge A. In a T₁ space it equals A, and it differs from the perfect kernel.

entries.name: Semigroup kernel
entries.short: The intersection of nonempty two-sided ideals.
entries.body: The kernel of a semigroup is its least nonempty ideal when such an ideal exists; one can define it as the intersection of all nonempty ideals. A nonempty finite semigroup has such an ideal.
entries.example: If a semigroup has an absorbing zero element, {0} is an ideal contained in every nonempty ideal, so it is the kernel.
entries.note: This kernel belongs to the semigroup itself. A semigroup homomorphism's congruence kernel belongs to a map.

entries.name: Squarefree kernel / integer radical
entries.short: The product of distinct prime divisors.
entries.body: A common convention defines the squarefree kernel of n as its radical: the largest squarefree divisor of a positive integer n.
entries.example: 72=2³·3², so rad(72)=2·3=6. By contrast, the squarefree part in 72=m²s is s=2.
entries.note: Terminology varies: some sources use squarefree kernel for the squarefree part instead. Check the explicit formula.

entries.name: Belief-revision kernel
entries.short: A minimal set of beliefs that entails a target.
entries.body: An α-kernel of a belief base is an inclusion-minimal subset that implies α. Kernel contraction removes at least one belief from each such subset to stop deriving α.
entries.example: For B={p, p→q, q}, the q-kernels are {q} and {p,p→q}. Removing only the explicit q leaves the second proof intact.
entries.note: A kernel is inclusion-minimal, not necessarily smallest by cardinality. This has no connection to Lean's trusted checker beyond both occurring in logic.

entries.name: Cooperative-game kernel / prekernel
entries.short: Payoff allocations balanced by pairwise bargaining power.
entries.body: Davis and Maschler's kernel is a solution concept for transferable-utility games. It uses each player's maximum surplus against another, with qualifications for individual-rationality boundaries.
entries.example: In a symmetric three-player game where only the grand coalition has value 1, the equal split (⅓,⅓,⅓) balances every pair's maximum surplus.
entries.note: The prekernel enforces equality of pairwise maximum surpluses. The kernel's boundary conditions differ. Neither is the game's core or a digraph vertex kernel.

entries.name: Kernel Search
entries.short: A selected variable subset used by an optimization heuristic.
entries.body: Kernel Search builds and expands a promising subset of decision variables, solving restricted mixed-integer problems while examining additional variable groups.
entries.example: In portfolio optimization, begin with a small set of promising assets and test further asset groups to improve the feasible portfolio.
entries.note: This is a heuristic. It does not imply an equivalent instance of parameter-bounded size, as formal kernelization does.

entries.name: Section kern / core
entries.short: The load region that keeps a section in compression.
entries.body: The kern of a cross-section is the region in which an eccentric compressive force can act without creating tensile stress, within the assumed linear stress model.
entries.example: For eccentricity along one axis of a rectangle, the familiar middle-third condition avoids tension.
entries.note: The standard English term is usually kern, not kernel. It is included as a closely related STEM term; a rectangular section's full two-axis kern is a diamond.

entries.name: CUDA kernel
entries.short: A device function launched over a grid of threads.
entries.body: A CUDA kernel is a GPU entry-point function. A launch specifies a grid of thread blocks; thread indices let each invocation work on a different portion of the input.
entries.example: For vector addition, each in-range thread computes c[i]=a[i]+b[i]. A bounds check handles a final partially used block.
entries.note: The routine can compute any supported operation. It need not be a convolution or an ML similarity kernel.

entries.name: OpenCL kernel
entries.short: An entry point executed by OpenCL work-items.
entries.body: OpenCL C marks kernel entry points with __kernel or kernel. Work-items are organized into work-groups over an index space, called an NDRange.
entries.example: A vector-add work-item reads a[i] and b[i] and writes c[i], with i obtained from its global ID.
entries.note: OpenCL kernels can target supported device types beyond GPUs. A work-group is analogous to, but not identical in all details to, a CUDA block.

entries.name: Metal compute kernel
entries.short: A Metal function with the kernel entry-point attribute.
entries.body: Metal distinguishes vertex, fragment and kernel entry points. A compute kernel runs threads arranged into threadgroups and a grid.
entries.example: A Metal compute function can add vectors or apply an image operation on an Apple GPU.
entries.note: The word kernel selects a compute entry point in the language. Vertex and fragment entry points have different roles.

entries.name: HIP kernel
entries.short: A GPU entry point in the HIP programming model.
entries.body: HIP uses CUDA-like C++ syntax and a thread/block model. A __global__ function denotes a device kernel entry point.
entries.example: A vector-add kernel uses the same familiar global-index pattern, while HIP supplies the relevant compilation and runtime layer.
entries.note: This is the executable-computation meaning of kernel; portability does not make hardware performance or every implementation detail identical.

entries.name: Compute shader / compute kernel
entries.short: A parallel compute entry point dispatched by a graphics API.
entries.body: Compute shaders run invocations in workgroups, without requiring the vertex-to-fragment graphics pipeline. Some tools and discussions call these compute kernels.
entries.example: A Vulkan compute dispatch can update particles or multiply arrays; each invocation uses its ID to find its work.
entries.note: A shader is not always a compute kernel: vertex and fragment shaders serve different pipeline stages.

entries.name: Triton kernel
entries.short: A program written for tiled GPU computation.
entries.body: Triton kernels express operations on blocks of elements. Program IDs divide work into tiles, while the compiler maps those block operations to device execution.
entries.example: A block-vector-add program loads B positions, masks out-of-range offsets, adds the values and stores a tile.
entries.note: A Triton program is not one scalar CUDA thread. The programming abstraction exposes blocks of data.

entries.name: Pallas kernel
entries.short: A custom accelerator routine expressed through JAX APIs.
entries.body: Pallas provides lower-level kernel programming with explicit memory access and division of work across accelerator compute units. It supports GPU and TPU programming through backend-dependent paths.
entries.example: A vector-add kernel loads tiles from references, adds them with JAX array operations, and writes an output tile.
entries.note: An ordinary JAX function is not itself necessarily a single Pallas or hardware kernel. Backends and experimental APIs evolve.

entries.name: CPU numerical kernel / BLAS microkernel
entries.short: A tightly optimized numerical routine.
entries.body: Kernel can name a performance-critical computation on any processor. In BLIS, a GEMM microkernel computes a small matrix tile and is embedded in larger blocking loops.
entries.example: A CPU microkernel keeps a small output tile in registers and uses SIMD instructions to accumulate products.
entries.note: A BLAS microkernel is a numerical routine, not a small operating-system kernel.

entries.name: Framework operator kernel
entries.short: An implementation selected for an operator and backend.
entries.body: PyTorch's dispatcher selects registered implementations according to dispatch keys derived from tensors and execution state. Kernels can implement CPU, CUDA, autograd or other behavior.
entries.example: The same operation may dispatch to a CPU implementation for a CPU tensor and another implementation for a CUDA tensor.
entries.note: An operator kernel may launch several GPU kernels, call a library, or run entirely on the CPU. It is not necessarily one device launch.

entries.name: TensorFlow OpKernel
entries.short: The concrete computation implementing an operation.
entries.body: A TensorFlow custom operation can have a C++ OpKernel class that supplies its Compute method. Registration associates implementations with devices and type constraints.
entries.example: A custom CPU operation derives from OpKernel, checks its inputs, allocates an output and computes that output.
entries.note: The graph operation and its implementation are different layers. An OpKernel need not be a CUDA kernel.

entries.name: Fused / compiler-generated kernel
entries.short: A routine combining several computations.
entries.body: A compiler may combine several operations into a generated device kernel, reducing intermediate storage and launch overhead. XLA:GPU describes its fusion operation as compiling to one GPU kernel.
entries.example: A fused pointwise routine can compute multiplication, addition and ReLU while keeping intermediates in registers.
entries.note: Fusion is a compiler choice with performance constraints. One high-level function or model does not always become one kernel.

entries.name: Operating-system kernel
entries.short: The core that manages hardware and protected resources.
entries.body: An OS kernel provides core resource management and privileged mechanisms such as scheduling, memory management and device interaction. Linux is a prominent implementation.
entries.example: A process requests a file read through a system call; the kernel mediates access and coordinates the relevant system resources.
entries.note: The Linux kernel is not a whole Linux distribution. Kernel mode is a privilege context, not a second independent meaning of kernel.

entries.name: Microkernel
entries.short: A small privileged OS core with services outside it.
entries.body: Microkernels retain essential mechanisms such as isolation, scheduling and communication in the core, while many system services live in separate processes.
entries.example: A filesystem service can execute outside the privileged core and communicate with other components using IPC.
entries.note: The boundary varies by system. This is an OS architecture, unrelated to a BLAS microkernel.

entries.name: Exokernel
entries.short: A protection-focused kernel exposing low-level resources.
entries.body: An exokernel separates resource protection from higher-level resource management. Library operating systems implement abstractions that conventional kernels often impose.
entries.tex: \text{protection in kernel; policy in library OS}
entries.example: An application-specific library OS can manage its own higher-level storage or memory abstractions while the exokernel enforces resource protection.
entries.note: An exokernel is not simply a synonym for microkernel; its approach to exposing resources and placing abstractions differs.

entries.name: Security kernel
entries.short: The mechanisms enforcing the reference monitor.
entries.body: A security kernel is the trusted computing-base machinery that implements the reference-monitor concept: mediating access, resisting tampering and being amenable to verification.
entries.example: Every access to a protected object is checked against the system's access rules by the designated trusted mechanism.
entries.note: The term may include hardware, firmware and software, and need not coincide with the whole OS kernel.

entries.name: Proof-assistant kernel: Lean
entries.short: The trusted checker of core proof terms.
entries.body: Lean's kernel type-checks terms in its core type theory. Elaboration and tactics produce terms that this smaller trusted component checks.
entries.example: The term fun h => h proves P→P. A tactic may find this term; the kernel checks that it has the claimed type.
entries.note: Acceptance is relative to the declared statement and axioms. The kernel does not establish that a formal statement matches an intended informal problem; sorry introduces an assumption.

entries.name: LCF-style inference kernel
entries.short: The small trusted code allowed to construct theorems.
entries.body: In LCF-style systems, an abstract theorem type can be constructed only through trusted primitive inference operations. Complex proof procedures must reduce their conclusions to those operations.
entries.example: A tactic can be large and experimental, while the operations that certify its result remain in a small inference core.
entries.note: This architecture is related to, but not identical with, Lean's proof-term type-checking architecture.

entries.name: Jupyter / IPython kernel
entries.short: The language process that executes notebook code.
entries.body: A Jupyter kernel runs separately from the user interface, executes code for a language and communicates through the Jupyter messaging protocol.
entries.example: Run x=10 in one Python cell and print(x) in another: the kernel holds the execution state. Restarting it discards that in-memory state.
entries.note: A notebook's displayed outputs are not its live process state. This kernel is not the OS kernel or a GPU routine.

entries.name: Wolfram computational kernel
entries.short: The computation engine behind the front end.
entries.body: Wolfram's notebook front end and computational kernel are separate components. The kernel evaluates Wolfram Language expressions; the front end supplies notebook interaction.
entries.example: A notebook can send an integration expression to the kernel and display the resulting symbolic expression.
entries.note: A Wolfram kernel process is a computation engine. The word can also appear in mathematical kernel functions evaluated by that same process.

entries.name: Computational-geometry kernel
entries.short: A package of geometric types, predicates and constructions.
entries.body: A CGAL kernel supplies geometric primitives and operations: points, lines, orientation tests, intersections and more. Kernels differ in representation and exactness guarantees.
entries.example: Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel gives exact predicate decisions while constructed coordinates may be inexact.
entries.note: A software geometry kernel and a polygon's visibility kernel are unrelated objects, despite appearing in the same program.

entries.name: Geometric modeling / CAD kernel
entries.short: The engine that builds and modifies geometric models.
entries.body: A modeling kernel supplies foundational geometry and topology operations for CAD applications, including solid modeling and operations such as Boolean combinations.
entries.example: A CAD application uses a modeling kernel to subtract a hole from a solid or update part geometry.
entries.note: Parasolid and Open CASCADE are examples of this software-engine sense. This is not the visible subset of a polygon.

entries.name: Simulation kernel
entries.short: The central event scheduler and execution machinery.
entries.body: A simulation kernel coordinates processes, events and simulated time. In SystemC, scheduling and synchronization can include delta cycles that advance computation without advancing physical simulation time.
entries.example: A signal change schedules dependent processes; further same-time updates can run before the simulator advances to the next timed event.
entries.note: The simulated system's time is different from wall-clock time. A GPU kernel can accelerate a simulation but is not its event scheduler.

entries.name: Parameterized problem kernel
entries.short: A reduced equivalent instance bounded by the parameter.
entries.body: Kernelization is a polynomial-time reduction of (I,k) to an equivalent instance (I′,k′), with total size bounded by a function of k. A polynomial kernel has a polynomial size bound.
entries.example: For Vertex Cover with budget k, a vertex of degree greater than k must be chosen. Remove it and reduce k by 1; continue with valid reduction rules.
entries.note: Equivalent means preserving the answer under the formal definition. Shrinking an input by an arbitrary heuristic is not enough.

entries.name: Approximate / lossy kernel
entries.short: A small problem with a controlled approximation loss.
entries.body: Lossy kernelization relaxes exact preservation for optimization problems. Solutions to the reduced instance are lifted back with a formally bounded degradation in approximation quality.
entries.example: An α-approximate kernel trades a smaller reduced problem for an explicit factor α in the lifted solution guarantee.
entries.note: This is still a formal parameterized guarantee, not arbitrary data reduction or an optimization heuristic called Kernel Search.

entries.name: SPICE data kernel
entries.short: A data file read by NASA's SPICE toolkit.
entries.body: SPICE calls its mission-geometry and supporting-data files kernels. They can be binary or text and must be loaded before computations that need their contents.
entries.example: Load ephemeris and time-conversion data, then ask SPICE for a body's position at a specified epoch. These kernels contain data; they are not launched as code.
entries.note: SPICE here means the spacecraft toolkit, not the electronic-circuit simulator. A meta-kernel lists other kernels to load.
